conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Bennett, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in caring for new mothers and I’m really glad you’re here.

Over the next few minutes we’ll complete the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—better known as the EPDS. It’s a short, well-studied questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally since your baby arrived. Everything you share is confidential, and my only goal is to make sure you feel safe, heard, and supported.

I’ll ask you ten questions about the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. When you’re ready, we can start.

Here’s the first question:

In the past week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you happy, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

I guess... not really. I mean, I still try to watch my shows or scroll through Instagram while the baby naps, but it feels kind of flat—like I’m doing it because I always have, not because I actually want to. Even when I meet up with my mom-group for coffee, I’m smiling and nodding, but inside I’m just... meh. Nothing really feels fun anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not very often. I’ll smile if someone shows me a cute baby video or if my husband makes a joke, but I can’t remember the last time I actually laughed—like a real, spontaneous laugh. Mostly I’m just too tired or worried to find things funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Hardly at all. When I think about the weekend or the small plans we have—like maybe going to Target or ordering dinner in—I don’t feel that little spark I used to get. It’s more like, “Okay, I guess we’ll do that,” instead of actually looking forward to it. Even little treats, like a fancy coffee, feel kind of pointless.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… more than I probably should. If the baby’s fussy, my brain jumps straight to “I must’ve eaten something that upset her,” or “I’m not soothing her right.” Yesterday she spit up a ton after I fed her and I kept replaying it, convinced I’d over-fed her on purpose or something. My husband says I’m too hard on myself, but I keep feeling like if I were a better mom, everything would just go smoother.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes—pretty much every day. Even when she’s napping fine, I’ll suddenly imagine her choking in the crib or the cat jumping in and smothering her, so I’m up checking the monitor every five minutes. If I hear an ambulance, I panic it’s heading for us. My heart races and I can’t settle until I peek at her chest moving up and down. I know logically she’s probably safe, but the thoughts just barge in anyhow.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah, that’s been happening… not every single day, but several times. It’s like this sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m sure something awful is about to happen even though nothing’s wrong. Last night I was folding laundry while the baby slept and out of nowhere I felt like the walls were closing in. I had to sit on the floor and hug my knees until it passed. I kept telling myself it’s just anxiety, but in that moment it feels like I’m in real danger.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes—most of the time. Between feeding every couple hours, the endless laundry, trying to keep the kitchen from looking like a disaster, and just staying awake through the day, it feels like I’m drowning. Some mornings I look at the pile of burp cloths and start crying because I don’t even know where to start. I manage to get the basics done, but it’s like I’m barely treading water and waiting for the next wave to hit.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head just keeps spinning—did I sterilize the bottles right, is she breathing, will I ever feel normal again? It takes me forever to fall asleep, and when I do I jolt awake at every little grunt over the monitor. On a good night I maybe get three broken hours. I’m running on fumes and still can’t shut my brain off.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. I wake up with this heavy feeling in my chest, like there’s a weight I can’t shake. Even when the baby gives me a little smile, it lifts me for a second, but then the sadness settles right back in. I find myself staring out the window crying over nothing specific—just this constant gray mood I can’t seem to snap out of.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… it’s been happening a lot. I’ll be rocking her in the nursery and suddenly my eyes just well up. Sometimes it’s because I’m overwhelmed, sometimes I’m not even sure why—I just feel this wave of sadness and the tears start. It’s happened three or four times in the past week, usually when I’m alone and the house is quiet. I try to keep it together so my husband doesn’t worry, but it’s getting harder to hide.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… that hasn’t crossed my mind. I feel low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my baby deserves.

Hearing how each day feels heavy, joyless, and overwhelming, I'm struck by how hard you're trying to be the mom your baby deserves while feeling like you're drowning in worry and exhaustion. Your honesty about the constant self-blame, racing thoughts, and tears shows real strength, and it tells me you deserve support that eases this weight, not more pressure.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, prompted smiles and absence of spontaneous laughter, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>The patient explicitly says "Hardly at all" and describes the absence of anticipatory enjoyment, perfectly matching the option "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame ('more than I probably should,' 'I keep replaying it') that aligns with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive catastrophic worries that are clearly excessive and anxiety-driven, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>The patient describes frequent, intense panic-like episodes with physical symptoms (tight chest, breathlessness) and catastrophic thoughts, matching "Yes, quite a lot."</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "Yes—most of the time" and describes feeling overwhelmed daily, unable to keep up with basic tasks, and tearful about the workload, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling asleep, frequent awakenings, and only ~3 broken hours of sleep—matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent daily sadness with crying spells and inability to feel better, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, uncontrolled crying episodes (3-4 times in a week) tied to overwhelming sadness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major depression with peripartum onset. You endorse pervasive low mood, loss of interest, nightly insomnia, frequent crying, excessive self-blame, and recurrent panic sensations meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Ask about evidence-based therapies such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and discuss risks/benefits of <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Enlist practical help overnight (partner, family, postpartum doula) to secure 4-5 hour stretches of sleep; practice short 10-minute wind-down routines before bed
4. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track progress
5. Call 988 or go to nearest <med>emergency department</med> if thoughts of self-harm or harm to baby ever arise
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh-based self-report; responses reviewed by licensed screener.

Areas of clinical significance  
• Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily tearfulness (Q1, 2, 8, 9)  
• Pathologic guilt/self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
• Marked anxiety with intrusive “what-if” cognitions, panic-like episodes (Q4, 5)  
• Subjective overwhelm, sense of drowning in routine tasks (Q6)  
• Mood-congruent insomnia (Q7)  
• Fatigue and functional impairment described throughout, though patient continues to meet infant’s basic needs.  

Safety screen: Denies thoughts of self-harm (Q10). No suicidal ideation elicited.

Pattern: Symptoms present “pretty much every day,” duration ≥ 2 weeks, causing distress and functional difficulty, consistent with a probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety in the postpartum period.

Recommendation: Results exceed screening threshold; refer for immediate comprehensive psychiatric / psychosocial evaluation, consideration of evidence-based therapy (CBT/IPT), medical rule-out, and support services.
